title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices
explain_beginner: AI systems are used in important areas, so people need reliable ways to judge what they can do and what risks they carry. Benchmarks are common tools for that, but this paper says they are not all equally trustworthy. The authors built a review method with 46 recommended practices covering a benchmark's whole life, then examined 24 benchmarks. They found wide quality differences, and many popular benchmarks have serious flaws. Most also fail to report whether results are statistically meaningful or make it easy for others to repeat the work. The paper offers a minimum quality checklist and a public assessment repository, so readers can check benchmarks before relying on their scores.
explain_business: AI benchmarks often guide model choices, progress tracking, and policy discussions, but this paper shows they vary greatly in quality. The authors reviewed 24 benchmarks using 46 recommended practices. Many widely used benchmarks have serious problems. Most do not show whether score differences are statistically meaningful, and most do not make results easy to reproduce. In practice, executives should treat benchmark scores as evidence that needs checking, not as final proof. The paper provides a minimum quality checklist and an online repository of reviews. These can help teams score benchmarks before choosing models or setting policy, and avoid relying on weak comparisons.
explain_practitioner: The authors created a structured way to judge AI benchmarks. It lists 46 recommended practices that span a benchmark's lifecycle. They applied this framework to 24 benchmarks. The evaluation showed substantial variation in quality, and several widely used benchmarks have notable problems. A common weakness is that results often lack statistical significance reporting. Another is that other teams usually cannot easily reproduce the findings. To help developers improve, the authors provide a checklist for basic quality checks. They also launched an ongoing public collection of benchmark reviews at betterbench.stanford.edu, which is meant to make different benchmarks easier to compare.
